name: Ngando-Lalia
confidence_why: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

Fuchu, Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. ISBN 978-4-86337-394-5. DOI 10.15026/125326.
catalog_locator: p. x, sec. 2.2.3 'Ton'; H/B 'ton ou morphotonème haut/bas' in 2.1 Abréviation p. viii; TAM tone formulas sec. 2.4.3 pp. xvi-xvii
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Kimura, Daiji & Lingomo Bongoli. 2023. Lexique longando / ロンガンド語彙集 [A Longando lexicon]. (Asian and African Lexicon, 65.) Fuchu, Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. xl + 541 pp. (584-page PDF). ISBN 978-4-86337-394-5. DOI 10.15026/125326.
tone_statements.quote: En longando, il y a essentiellement deux tons, un ton haut (´) et un ton bas (`). (Cependant, les symboles de tons bas sont généralement omis.) Par exemple, les trois mots suivants comportant des tons différents sont des mots différents : bókáká (façon de mourir avec un corps devenu dur), bókáka (grippe, épidémie), bókaka (cassure, fente, lézarde)
tone_statements.translation: In Longando there are essentially two tones, a high tone (´) and a low tone (`). (However, low-tone symbols are generally omitted.) For example, the following three words carrying different tones are different words: bókáká (way of dying with the body gone stiff), bókáka (flu, epidemic), bókaka (break, crack, fissure).
tone_statements.locator: p. x, sec. 2.2.3 'Ton'; grammatical tone formulas p. xvi sec. 2.4.3 'Temp[s]'; Japanese parallel text p. xxviii sec. 2.2.3 声調
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, H and L (L unmarked), lexically contrastive on the syllable (minimal triplet), with H/L morphotonemes on the verb prefix distinguishing TAM forms (grammatical tone); no statement on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Motingea Mangulu, André. 2000. La langue des Bongando septentrionaux (bantou C.63). Annales Aequatoria 21: 91-158.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 Tons pp. 104-105: two basic tones H/L plus falling/rising contours, lexical and grammatical function; 2.5 La syllabe p. 105: open syllables V, CV, CSV, syllabic N; 2.1.4 p. 97 vowel length only from coalescence/consonant loss. No accent/stress statement in the article.

sources.note: Checked (downloaded to scratch, not kept): pan-Mongo dialectology; phonology part has Tonologie/Intonation but no accent chapter; the one 'accent dynamique' remark (p. 253) concerns dialect 132, not a Bongando dialect (170-182, 200-221).

sources.citation: Vinck, Honoré. 1993. Bibliographie des Bongando. Annales Aequatoria 14: 585-593.
sources.note: Bibliography only; sec. B Linguistique p. 589 lists as published linguistic works only Hulstaert 1987 and Walling 1937, plus MS grammar notes (Gutersohn) and vocabularies (Cardinal, Mazy).

sources.citation: Kimura, Daiji. 1990. Verbal interaction of the Bongando in central Zaire: with special reference to their addressee-unspecified loud speech. African Study Monographs 11(1): 1-26.
sources.note: Anthropological; states 'Longando is a tonal language' and that loud-speech/whistled messages are understood from the H/L tone sequence alone; transcription marks tone and loudness; nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Hulstaert, Gustaaf. 1987. Les parlers des Bongandó méridionaux. Annales Aequatoria 8: 205-288.
sources.note: Ch. I Phonologie pp. 209-213 covers vowels, consonants, devocalisation, tones (D, pp. 211-212: tonal particularities vs other Mongo dialects, radical-tone lowering in conjugation, pausal lowering at end of declaratives), tonal assimilation, elisions. Nothing on accent/stress anywhere in the article (only 'particule d'intensité' ndé/nko in the morphology).
